text: Chapter 4 translated the five-layer adaptive architecture into working software, describing the implementation of each adaptive layer, the knowledge graph, the frontend dashboards, and the deployment configuration. Feature flags built into the AI service allow individual layers to be toggled on or off at runtime  --  a capability that proves essential in this chapter. The present chapter shifts from construction to validation: it describes the research methodology, experiment design, and evaluation metrics that will be used to determine whether the adaptive platform delivers on the learning improvements that its theoretical design anticipates. Four research questions, originally introduced in Section 1.4 and consolidated from five to four during the evaluation planning phase, guide the investigation. RQ1 asks whether the multi-layer adaptive system can accurately model student knowledge and predict performance. RQ2 examines whether Hierarchical MAB problem selection improves learning outcomes compared to content-based filtering. RQ3 investigates whether FSRS-based spaced repetition scheduling improves long-term retention of programming concepts. RQ4 assesses student perceptions of the platform's usability and usefulness. The evaluation employs a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative system metrics with qualitative survey and interview data to address these questions from complementary angles.

text: The evaluation of the adaptive learning platform follows a mixed-methods research design that integrates quantitative and qualitative data collection. The quantitative strand draws on two sources: (a) system-generated logs that capture every submission, recommendation, and adaptive state update during the intervention period, and (b) pre-test and post-test instruments that measure knowledge gain and retention. The qualitative strand comprises the System Usability Scale (SUS) questionnaire CITE1, a Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) survey CITE2, and semi-structured interviews analyzed through thematic analysis CITE3. This triangulation of data sources ensures that the evaluation captures not only measurable learning outcomes but also the subjective student experience that influences platform adoption in a real university setting.

text: - Experimental group (E): The full adaptive platform with all five layers active  --  Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (Layer 1), Dynamic Elo difficulty calibration (Layer 2), Hierarchical MAB problem selection (Layer 3), FSRS spaced repetition scheduling (Layer 4), and LLM-powered Socratic hints (Layer 5). - Control group (C): The same platform interface with all adaptive layers disabled. Problem recommendations are generated by the legacy content-based filtering system (cosine similarity over sentence-transformer embeddings). Students in the control group see the same problem set, use the same code execution sandbox, and access the same basic statistics dashboard, but receive no knowledge tracing, no Elo-based difficulty matching, no spaced repetition scheduling, and no adaptive hints.

text: The study adheres to standard ethical guidelines for educational research. All participants provide written informed consent before enrollment, with the consent form explaining the study's purpose, data collection procedures, and the right to withdraw at any time without academic penalty. Participation is entirely voluntary and carries no effect on course grades. Student identifiers are replaced with randomly generated codes during the data export phase, and all analysis is performed on anonymized datasets. Raw data is retained for two years following the study's completion and then permanently deleted. To ensure fairness, students in the control group are granted full access to the adaptive features after the experiment concludes. An ethics approval application is submitted to the Hanoi University institutional review board prior to participant recruitment.

text: The target sample comprises 40 to 60 students enrolled in programming courses at Hanoi University's Faculty of Information Technology. Eligible courses include Introduction to Programming, Data Structures, and Algorithms  --  all of which involve Python as the primary language and align with the 28-concept knowledge graph constructed in Section 4.2.

text: Inclusion criteria. Participants must satisfy three conditions: (a) current enrollment in one of the eligible programming courses, (b) ability to access the web-based platform from a personal computer or university laboratory, and (c) provision of written informed consent.

text: Exclusion criteria. Two categories of students are excluded: (a) those with prior competitive programming experience, operationally defined as an estimated Elo equivalent exceeding 1600, as such students are unlikely to benefit from or be appropriately challenged by the introductory-to-intermediate problem set; and (b) those unable to commit to four weeks of regular platform use.

text: Sample size justification. A priori power analysis using G*Power for an independent-samples t-test, with a medium effect size (Cohen's MATH1), significance level MATH2, and statistical power MATH3, yields a required sample of 26 participants per group CITE4. To accommodate an expected dropout rate of approximately 20%, the target enrollment is 30 participants per group, for a total of 60.

To accommodate an expected dropout rate of approximately 20%, the target enrollment is 30 participants per group, for a total of 60.

text: Contingency for smaller samples. If recruitment yields only 20 to 30 total participants (10 to 15 per group), the statistical approach is adjusted accordingly. At this sample size, only large effects (MATH1) can be detected with 80% power. The analysis plan shifts to non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U) that are more robust at small MATH2, and supplementary within-group evidence is strengthened: detailed per-student BKT and Elo convergence curves, per-concept mastery progression trajectories, and system log analysis of recommendation acceptance patterns. Under this scenario, the contribution is reframed from demonstrating a statistically significant group difference to providing a comprehensive demonstration of the integrated adaptive system with preliminary effectiveness evidence. Additionally, all participants are interviewed rather than a subset, enriching the qualitative analysis.

text: Randomization. Assignment to experimental and control groups uses stratified randomization by pre-test score. Pre-test scores are divided into terciles (low, medium, high), and within each tercile, students are randomly assigned to one of the two groups. This stratification ensures that baseline ability is balanced across conditions, preventing a scenario in which one group contains a disproportionate number of high- or low-performing students.

text: The experiment spans eight weeks divided into four phases: baseline assessment, intervention, post-assessment, and retention testing. Figure 5.1 illustrates the timeline, and Table 5.2 summarizes the feature differences between the experimental and control conditions.

text: Week 1: Baseline and setup. The first week consists of four activities conducted over consecutive days. Day 1 is an information session during which the study objectives, timeline, and data handling procedures are explained, followed by the collection of signed informed consent forms (approximately 30 minutes). Day 2 is the pre-test: a 60-minute assessment consisting of 20 questions  --  four at each of five difficulty levels  --  covering variables, control flow, functions, data structures, and basic algorithms. The pre-test uses a mix of multiple-choice and short-answer items and is auto-graded to ensure objective scoring. Day 3 begins with system onboarding: account creation and a guided tutorial of the platform interface (approximately 30 minutes). On the same day, stratified randomization is performed using the pre-test scores. Days 4 and 5 constitute a free exploration period during which students may use the platform without formal requirements, allowing them to familiarize themselves with the interface before the intervention begins.

text: Weeks 2--5: Intervention. During the four-week intervention period, both groups use the platform regularly. A minimum engagement requirement of three problems per week is communicated to all participants; students who fall below this threshold are flagged but not excluded from the primary analysis, which follows an intent-to-treat protocol. Table 5.2 details the feature differences between conditions.

text: The system collects six categories of data throughout the intervention. First, all submission events are logged with timestamps, code content, correctness verdict, attempt number, and time spent. Second, all recommendation events record the problems presented, their ordering, and the reason for inclusion (new practice, review, or exploration). Third, click events capture which recommendations were selected and their position in the list. Fourth, page views and session durations are recorded for engagement analysis. Fifth, for the experimental group, daily snapshots of BKT knowledge states are stored. Sixth, Elo rating histories and FSRS review events are logged for the experimental group to support the convergence and retention analyses required by RQ1 and RQ3.

text: Week 6: Post-assessment. The post-assessment phase mirrors the pre-test in structure. On Day 1, participants complete the post-test: a parallel-form instrument covering the same topics and difficulty distribution as the pre-test but with different questions to avoid test-retest effects. On Day 2, participants complete the SUS questionnaire (approximately 10 minutes) and the TAM questionnaire (approximately 10 minutes). On Day 3, semi-structured interviews are conducted with a stratified subsample of 10 students from each group, selected to represent high, medium, and low learning gain as measured by the difference between pre-test and post-test scores. Each interview lasts approximately 20 minutes. By Day 5, all data is exported and anonymized.

text: Week 8: Retention test. Two weeks after the intervention ends, all participants complete a 10-question retention test covering a subset of the concepts addressed during the intervention. Only concepts that were classified as mastered (BKT MATH1) during the intervention are eligible for retention testing. This two-week gap, while short for a full evaluation of spaced repetition, provides the minimum viable window to detect divergence in FSRS stability values between conditions CITE2. Participants are reminded of the retention test three days and one day in advance. The retention test is classified as committed rather than optional: without it, only short-term learning improvement can be claimed, and RQ3 cannot be adequately addressed.

text: Dependent variables. The dependent variables span four categories aligned with the research questions. For learning effectiveness (RQ2): Normalized Learning Gain and Problems-to-Mastery ratio. For model accuracy (RQ1): BKT prediction AUC-ROC, Elo prediction AUC-ROC, and Elo convergence speed. For engagement: session frequency, session duration, problems per session, voluntary return rate, dropout rate, and abandonment rate. For usability (RQ4): SUS composite score and TAM subscale means for Perceived Usefulness and Perceived Ease of Use.

text: Covariates. Three covariates are measured to control for individual differences: (a) the pre-test score, which serves as a baseline knowledge measure and is used for stratified randomization; (b) prior programming experience, assessed through a self-report item on the consent form (categories: none, less than six months, six months to one year, more than one year); and (c) course enrollment level, distinguishing between introductory programming and intermediate courses (data structures or algorithms). These covariates are included in regression models to improve the precision of treatment effect estimates and to explore whether the adaptive system benefits certain subgroups more than others.

text: System Usability Scale (SUS). The SUS is a 10-item questionnaire that yields a composite score on a 0--100 scale CITE7. Originally developed by Brooke (1996), the SUS has been extensively validated across domains and is widely used in software evaluation. Following the adjective rating benchmarks established by Bangor et al. (2008), scores are interpreted as: not acceptable (MATH1), marginal (MATH2--MATH3), good (MATH4--MATH5), and excellent (MATH6). The target for this study is a mean SUS score of at least 70 for the experimental group. SUS scores are compared between the experimental and control groups using an independent-samples t-test, as SUS composite scores are generally normally distributed in samples of this size.
original: **System Usability Scale (SUS).** The SUS is a 10-item questionnaire that yields a composite score on a 0--100 scale [51]. Originally developed by Brooke (1996), the SUS has been extensively validated across domains and is widely used in software evaluation. Following the adjective rating benchmarks established by Bangor et al. (2008), scores are interpreted as: not acceptable ($< 50$), marginal ($50$--$70$), good ($70$--$85$), and excellent ($> 85$). The target for this study is a mean SUS score of at least 70 for the experimental group. SUS scores are compared between the experimental and control groups using an independent-samples t-test, as SUS composite scores are generally normally distributed in samples of this size.

text: - Perceived Usefulness (PU): Six items rated on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree), measuring the degree to which students believe the adaptive features improved their learning experience. Sample item: "The adaptive recommendations helped me learn programming more effectively." - Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU): Six items on the same 7-point Likert scale, measuring how easy students found the adaptive interface to use. Sample item: "The difficulty indicators were clear and helpful."

text: Internal consistency of each subscale is assessed using Cronbach's MATH1, with a threshold of MATH2 considered acceptable. The target for both PU and PEOU is a mean score of at least 5.0 on the 7-point scale. Subscale means are compared between groups using independent-samples t-tests.

text: Semi-Structured Interviews. Qualitative data from the 20 semi-structured interviews (10 per group) is analyzed using thematic analysis following the six-phase approach of Braun and Clarke CITE1: familiarization with transcripts, initial coding, theme generation, theme review, theme definition, and reporting. Interview questions are designed to elicit responses about problem selection behavior, perceived difficulty calibration, progress awareness, and platform improvement suggestions. Themes emerging from the experimental group are compared with those from the control group to identify qualitative differences in learning experience attributable to the adaptive features.

text: For each quantitative metric listed in Table 5.3, the following analysis protocol is applied. First, normality of the distribution within each group is assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Second, homogeneity of variance is tested using Levene's test. If both assumptions are met, an independent-samples t-test is used for the between-group comparison; if normality is violated, the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test is applied; if only the variance assumption is violated, Welch's t-test is used. All comparisons report the test statistic, MATH1-value, 95% confidence interval, and an effect size measure (Cohen's MATH2 or Hedges' MATH3 for small samples). To control the family-wise error rate across the four primary comparisons (one per research question), the Bonferroni correction is applied, yielding an adjusted significance threshold of MATH4. Secondary and exploratory analyses  --  such as per-concept learning gain and engagement comparisons  --  are reported without correction but are explicitly flagged as exploratory. Missing data is handled through an intent-to-treat approach for the primary analysis, with a per-protocol sensitivity analysis restricted to participants who met the minimum engagement requirement of three problems per week.
